newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea opposition leader warns of economic crisis.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea opposition leader warns of economic crisis.

text.p: South Korea's main opposition leader warned on Monday the country was facing economic crisis, and chairmen of big industrial conglomerates prepared unprecedented joint action to freeze wages.
"Our economy is now in a total crisis due to the government's inconsistent economic policies," Kim Dae-jung, head of the National Congress for New Politics, told a news conference.

Chairmen of the top 30 business groups, or chaebol, are expected to agree on Tuesday to freeze overall spending on salaries and benefits next year, a move that almost certainly will spark a showdown with powerful unions.
They are also likely to endorse early retirement schemes. South Korean labour law makes it virtually impossible to forcibly lay off workers.
"The sense of crisis is based on a recognition that the economic downdurn is structural and not cyclical," said Yoo Byung-kook, an economist at Hyundai Research Institute.
"A salary freeze can be the right medicine for the current economic malaise, which mainly stems from higher wage increases than productivity rises."
Average pay has risen by 15 percent annually since 1987, outpacing productivity by two to three percentage points.

Other analysts, however, said a wage freeze would unfairly penalise workers for problems of industrial overcapacity created by management. It might even spark a recession by dampening domestic household consumption.
"Only household consumption remains healthy; squashing it could plunge the economy into a true recession," Steve Marvin, head of research at Ssangyong Securities, wrote in a recent report.
Analysts said a wage freeze and moves to trim corporate workforces could trigger more problems unless the government convinces people that everyone will suffer equally.
"Labour unions won't sit idly by if they feel they are the only party deprived in the campaign," said Yoo.
Kim, in a clear reference to moves by the conglomerates to freeze wages, said workers should not be made to suffer.
"It is not fair to demand workers' sacrifice. We have no right to blame their right to demand their fair share within productivity increase," he said.
Instead, he urged the government to tighten its belt by lowering the growth of its budget spending next year to 11 percent from a proposed 14 percent.

"The government should initiate a frugality drive to overcome the current economic crisis," he said, proposing that several ministries should be axed, including the ministries of interior and information.
South Korea's economy has been hit by plunging world prices for its main exports, including semiconductors, steel and petrochemical products.
Profits of 415 listed manufacturing firms slumped by 53.17 percent in the first half.
Kim said the current economic difficulties necessitated a delay in joining the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
"The government's plan to join the OECD should be delayed by two to three years given the economic weakness," Kim said.

South Korea is hoping the OECD governing council will approve its membership at a meeting on September 26. Opposition parties have opposed market-opening measures to gain acceptance to the Paris-based club of rich nations.
